clusters.title: Datasets and Variable Types
clusters.reasoning: Rows/columns and variable types are two facets of the same foundational idea — what a dataset looks like and what kind of values it holds. A learner encounters both simultaneously when first opening a dataset. Neither requires the other as a prerequisite; they read as complementary parts of one orientation.

clusters.title: Data Quality and the Analysis Workflow
clusters.reasoning: Data quality is a prerequisite concern that feeds directly into the analysis workflow — understanding what makes data trustworthy is part of understanding the workflow itself. These two concepts read as steps of one process. Ethics/privacy is a distinct conceptual domain (legal and ethical obligations) that learners must learn to separate from the technical workflow, so it is not clustered here.

clusters.title: Variables and Core Data Types
clusters.reasoning: Variable assignment and core data types are inseparable in Python: every assignment creates a typed value. Learners encounter both in the same first code cell. They read as two aspects of one idea — naming and typing values.

clusters.title: Comparison and Logical Operators
clusters.reasoning: Comparison and logical operators are always used together to build compound conditions (e.g., x > 0 and x < 10). They form one idea: constructing boolean tests. Arithmetic operators produce numbers rather than booleans and are a distinct concept; type_conversion is a separate operation. Clustering only comparison and logical keeps the important boundary between numeric and boolean operations visible.

clusters.title: Lists, Dictionaries, and Tuples
clusters.reasoning: Lists, dictionaries, and tuples are Python's three core built-in collection types. Showing them together makes the key distinctions immediately visible: lists are ordered and mutable, tuples are ordered and immutable, dictionaries are key-value mappings. Learners need to choose between them in practice, and the contrast is the core learning. They read as three variants of one idea: storing multiple values in Python.

clusters.title: Conditionals and For Loops
clusters.reasoning: Conditionals and for loops are the two foundational control flow structures in Python, and they are routinely combined (a for loop containing an if statement). They read as complementary parts of one idea: directing program flow. Neither requires the other as a prerequisite at the tile's start.

clusters.title: While Loops and Loop Control
clusters.reasoning: Loop control statements (break, continue, pass) are only meaningful inside a loop. While loops and loop control read as one idea: how to run and exit a loop conditionally. They are always taught together.

clusters.title: Comprehensions and Iterating Collections
clusters.reasoning: List comprehensions are a compact syntax for iterating over a collection and transforming it — they are the same idea expressed differently. Showing them together lets learners see the equivalence between a for-loop iteration and a comprehension, which is the core insight of this tile.

clusters.title: Defining Functions, Parameters, and Return Values
clusters.reasoning: Defining a function, passing parameters, and returning values are the three inseparable parts of a function's basic interface. A learner cannot understand any one of them without the other two — they form a single mental model: 'a function takes inputs and produces an output.' Default/keyword arguments are a parameter variant that builds on this foundation and is better shown separately. Variable scope is a distinct concept about name resolution.

clusters.title: Measures of Center and Spread
clusters.reasoning: Measures of center (mean, median, mode) and measures of spread (variance, standard deviation, IQR) are the two complementary halves of descriptive statistics — they answer 'where is the data?' and 'how spread out is it?' respectively. They are always interpreted together and form one idea: summarizing a distribution numerically.

clusters.title: Distribution Shape, Outliers, and Frequency Distributions
clusters.reasoning: Reading a frequency distribution, identifying its shape (symmetric, skewed, bimodal), and reasoning about outliers are three steps of one analytical act: understanding how a variable is distributed. A learner cannot reason about outliers without first understanding shape, and shape is read from a frequency distribution. They form a single workflow and are always taught together.

clusters.title: Correlation and Its Limits
clusters.reasoning: Correlation, how to interpret the correlation coefficient, and the correlation-vs-causation caveat are three aspects of one concept. A learner who knows what correlation is but not how to interpret r, or who doesn't know the causation caveat, has an incomplete and potentially dangerous understanding. Showing them together as a cluster makes the complete picture visible while keeping each sub-concept individually addressable.

clusters.title: DataFrames, Series, and Reading Data
clusters.reasoning: The DataFrame/Series model is the conceptual foundation for all pandas work, and reading data (pd.read_csv) is the first operation that produces a DataFrame. A learner needs the model to understand what read_csv returns. These two concepts are the entry point to pandas and read as one idea: what a DataFrame is and how to get one.

clusters.title: Creating and Inspecting DataFrames
clusters.reasoning: Creating a DataFrame and inspecting it (head, info, describe, shape) are the first two steps of every pandas workflow — you create or load data, then immediately examine it. They read as a single orientation step: 'make a DataFrame and look at it.'

clusters.title: Selecting and Filtering Data
clusters.reasoning: loc/iloc (label/position-based selection) and boolean filtering (condition-based selection) are the two primary ways to select subsets of a DataFrame. Showing them together makes the contrast clear: one selects by address, the other by condition. They are variants of one operation — subsetting data — and learners need both to work effectively.

clusters.title: Type Conversion and Datetime Handling
clusters.reasoning: dtype conversion (astype, pd.to_numeric) and datetime handling (pd.to_datetime, dt accessor) are both about correcting column types in a DataFrame. Datetime conversion is the most common and complex type conversion case. They read as two aspects of one task: making sure columns have the right type before analysis.

clusters.title: Text Cleaning, Duplicates, and Missing Data
clusters.reasoning: String cleaning, removing duplicates, and handling missing values are the three main data cleaning operations in pandas. They address different problems but are always applied in the same cleaning phase of an analysis workflow. Showing them as a cluster lets learners see the full cleaning toolkit at once, with each operation individually addressable.

clusters.title: Mapping and Applying Transformations
clusters.reasoning: map (for substituting values via a dictionary or function on a Series) and apply (for applying a function element-wise or row/column-wise) are two variants of the same idea: transforming values in a DataFrame. Showing them together makes the distinction clear — map is for simple substitution, apply is for custom logic.

clusters.title: Concatenating and Merging DataFrames
clusters.reasoning: concat (stacking DataFrames by rows or columns) and merge (joining DataFrames on a key) are the two ways to combine DataFrames in pandas. Showing them together makes the fundamental distinction clear: concat stacks, merge joins. They are variants of one operation — combining DataFrames — and learners need to choose between them in practice.

clusters.title: The Relational Model and SELECT Basics
clusters.reasoning: The relational model (tables, rows, columns, relationships) is the conceptual foundation for SQL, and SELECT is the first query that retrieves from it. A learner needs the model to understand what SELECT returns. These two concepts are the entry point to SQL and read as one idea: what a relational database is and how to query it.

clusters.title: Filtering Rows with WHERE and Logical Operators
clusters.reasoning: WHERE and logical operators (AND, OR, NOT) are inseparable in practice — every non-trivial WHERE clause uses logical operators to combine conditions. They read as one idea: constructing a row filter. NULL handling involves three-valued logic (TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN) which is a distinct and often surprising concept that learners must understand on its own terms, so it is not clustered here.

clusters.title: Sorting and Limiting Results
clusters.reasoning: ORDER BY and LIMIT/OFFSET are always used together to sort a result set and then take a slice of it (e.g., 'top 10 by revenue'). They read as two parts of one idea: controlling which rows appear in the output and in what order.

clusters.title: Aggregating Data with GROUP BY
clusters.reasoning: Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG), GROUP BY, and HAVING are the three components of the SQL aggregation pattern. GROUP BY groups rows, aggregate functions summarize each group, and HAVING filters the groups. A learner cannot use any one of them effectively without understanding the others — they form a single mental model: 'group rows and summarize each group, optionally filtering groups.'

clusters.title: Text and Date Functions
clusters.reasoning: String functions (UPPER, LOWER, TRIM, SUBSTRING, CONCAT) and date/time functions (DATE_TRUNC, EXTRACT, DATEDIFF) are both categories of scalar functions that transform column values in SELECT. They are often used together in data cleaning and reporting queries. Type casting (CAST, ::) is a distinct operation about converting between data types and is better shown separately.

clusters.title: Entities, Tables, and Primary Keys
clusters.reasoning: Entities/tables and primary keys are inseparable in the relational model — a primary key is what uniquely identifies each row in a table and makes it a proper entity. A learner cannot understand what a table represents without understanding primary keys. They read as two aspects of one idea: what a table is and how rows are identified.

clusters.title: Foreign Keys and One-to-Many Relationships
clusters.reasoning: Foreign keys are the mechanism that implements one-to-many relationships — a foreign key in the 'many' table points to the primary key in the 'one' table. These two concepts are two sides of the same coin: the relationship pattern and the column that enforces it. They are always taught together in data modeling.

clusters.title: Normalization and Many-to-Many Relationships
clusters.reasoning: Normalization (reducing redundancy by splitting data into related tables) and many-to-many junction tables (the normalization technique for many-to-many relationships) are tightly linked. A junction table is the canonical example of normalization in action. They read as two aspects of one idea: how to structure data to avoid redundancy.

clusters.title: Query Execution Order and Subqueries in WHERE
clusters.reasoning: SQL clause execution order (FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY) directly explains why subqueries can appear in WHERE: the subquery runs first, producing a value that WHERE can filter on. Understanding execution order is the prerequisite mental model for understanding subquery placement. These two concepts read as one idea: how SQL processes a query and how that enables subqueries.

clusters.title: Subqueries in FROM and Common Table Expressions
clusters.reasoning: Subqueries in FROM (derived tables) and CTEs (WITH clause) are two syntactic approaches to the same idea: creating a named intermediate result set that the outer query can reference. CTEs are the modern, more readable alternative to subqueries in FROM. Showing them together makes the equivalence and the trade-offs immediately clear.

clusters.title: The Spreadsheet Grid and Cell References
clusters.reasoning: The spreadsheet grid model (rows, columns, cells) and cell references/ranges (A1, B2:D5) are inseparable — cell references are the addressing system for the grid. A learner cannot write a formula without understanding both. They read as two aspects of one foundational idea: how a spreadsheet is structured and how to point to locations in it.

clusters.title: Structured Tables and Named Ranges
clusters.reasoning: Structured tables (Excel Tables / Google Sheets tables with auto-expanding references) and named ranges are both mechanisms for giving a data region a meaningful name that can be referenced in formulas. They read as two variants of one idea: naming data regions to make formulas more readable and maintainable.

clusters.title: Sorting and Filtering Data
clusters.reasoning: Sorting (reordering rows by a column) and filtering (showing only rows that match a condition) are the two basic data exploration operations in a spreadsheet. They are always taught together and are often used in sequence: filter to a subset, then sort within it. They read as two parts of one idea: navigating and exploring tabular data.

clusters.title: Removing Duplicates and Splitting Text
clusters.reasoning: Removing duplicates and splitting text (Text to Columns / SPLIT) are both data cleaning operations applied to raw imported data. They are often used in sequence when cleaning a dataset: split combined fields, then remove duplicate rows. Cross-sheet references are a formula navigation concept and belong to a different idea.

clusters.title: Writing Formulas and Reference Types
clusters.reasoning: Formula syntax (= sign, operators, function calls) and relative/absolute references ($A$1 vs A1) are inseparable — every formula uses references, and whether those references are relative or absolute determines how the formula behaves when copied. They read as two aspects of one idea: how to write a formula correctly.

clusters.title: Text Combining and Text Extraction
clusters.reasoning: Text combining (CONCAT, TEXTJOIN, &) and text extraction (LEFT, RIGHT, MID, FIND) are two complementary text manipulation operations — one builds strings from parts, the other pulls parts from strings. They are variants of one idea: working with text values in formulas, and are often used together when cleaning or reformatting text data.

clusters.title: VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP and INDEX/MATCH
clusters.reasoning: VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP and INDEX/MATCH are the two main lookup approaches in spreadsheets. Showing them together makes the trade-offs immediately clear: VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP is simpler but limited to left-to-right lookups; INDEX/MATCH is more flexible. Learners need to choose between them in practice. Formula error troubleshooting is a debugging skill that applies to all formulas and is better shown separately.

clusters.title: Building and Summarizing Pivot Tables
clusters.reasoning: Building a pivot table (inserting, configuring rows/columns/values) and summarizing with it (choosing aggregation functions, filtering, grouping) are two steps of one workflow. A learner cannot summarize with a pivot table without first building one. They read as the setup and the use of the same tool.

clusters.title: Figures, Layout, and Basic Plotting
clusters.reasoning: The Figure/Axes model, figure size and layout configuration, and basic pyplot plotting are three aspects of the same setup: creating a matplotlib figure. A learner needs all three to produce their first plot. They read as the initialization steps of any matplotlib visualization and are always taught together.

clusters.title: Bar Charts and Histograms
clusters.reasoning: Bar charts (categorical comparison) and histograms (continuous distribution) are often confused because they look similar. Showing them together makes the critical distinction immediately visible: bar charts have gaps between bars and compare categories; histograms have no gaps and show distribution. The contrast is the core learning, making them ideal for a cluster.

clusters.title: Line Plots and Scatter Plots
clusters.reasoning: Line plots (trends over an ordered axis, typically time) and scatter plots (relationship between two continuous variables) are both two-variable charts that learners often conflate. Showing them together makes the distinction clear: line plots connect ordered points to show trend; scatter plots show correlation between unordered pairs. Box plots show distribution rather than relationships and are better shown separately.

clusters.title: Seaborn DataFrame Plotting and Statistical Functions
clusters.reasoning: Seaborn's DataFrame-aware plotting (sns.barplot, sns.scatterplot) and its statistical functions (sns.histplot with kde, sns.regplot, sns.boxplot) are two levels of the same library: basic chart creation and statistically-enhanced chart creation. They read as two aspects of one idea: using seaborn to visualize data. Themes and palettes are a styling concern that applies after the chart is created.

clusters.title: A/B Test Structure and Lift
clusters.reasoning: A/B test structure (control vs treatment, random assignment, metric selection) and lift interpretation (the relative improvement of treatment over control) are two aspects of the same experiment: how to design it and how to read its primary result. A learner cannot interpret lift without understanding the test structure that produced it.

clusters.title: Sample Size, Effect Size, and Statistical Significance
clusters.reasoning: Sample size/effect size and statistical significance/confidence intervals are two interconnected statistical concepts for evaluating experiment validity. Sample size determines whether an effect can be detected; significance tells you whether the detected effect is likely real. They are always interpreted together and form one idea: 'is this result trustworthy?' Business conclusions from experiments are the translation step that applies these concepts to a decision, and are better shown separately.

clusters.title: Identifying Decisions, Findings, and Requirements
clusters.reasoning: Identifying the decision need, stating findings precisely, framing the analytical question, and identifying requirements are four sequential steps of the same pre-analysis phase: understanding what the stakeholder actually needs before any data is touched. They read as one process — scoping the work — and are always addressed together in stakeholder conversations. Each step builds on the previous one.

clusters.title: Recommendations and Plain-Language Translation
clusters.reasoning: Forming a data-driven recommendation and translating it into plain language are two steps of the same communication act: deciding what to say and then saying it in terms the stakeholder understands. A recommendation that cannot be translated into plain language is not yet complete. They read as two parts of one idea: communicating a finding as an actionable recommendation.

clusters.title: Prioritizing Findings and Framing Recommendations
clusters.reasoning: Prioritizing findings by relevance (selecting which results matter most to the stakeholder) and framing recommendations as actionable (stating what to do, not just what was found) are two aspects of the same editorial decision: what to lead with and how to say it. Narrative context setup is about structuring the opening of a presentation, which is a distinct communication skill.

clusters.title: Tailoring Detail and Anticipating Questions
clusters.reasoning: Tailoring the level of detail to the audience and anticipating their questions and objections are two aspects of audience-aware communication. Both require the analyst to model the stakeholder's perspective: what do they need to know, and what will they push back on? They read as two parts of one idea: preparing a presentation for a specific audience.

clusters.title: Matching and Simplifying Charts for an Audience
clusters.reasoning: Choosing the right chart type for the point being made and simplifying charts for a non-technical audience are two aspects of the same skill: making a visualization communicate clearly. They read as two parts of one idea: chart design for stakeholder communication.

clusters.title: Structuring Presentations and Writing Executive Summaries
clusters.reasoning: Presentation structure (opening, findings, recommendation, appendix) and executive summary writing (one-page distillation of the key finding and recommendation) are two formats for the same communication goal: delivering analytical results to a stakeholder. They read as two variants of one idea: how to organize and present findings.

clusters.title: Defining the Question and Planning the Workflow
clusters.reasoning: Defining the business question, selecting the data retrieval method, and structuring the end-to-end workflow are three sequential planning steps for a capstone project. They form one idea: scoping and planning an analysis before executing it. A learner cannot choose a retrieval method without a defined question, and cannot structure the workflow without knowing both.

clusters.title: Integrating SQL, Spreadsheets, and pandas
clusters.reasoning: Integrating SQL, spreadsheets, and pandas are three parallel tool-application steps in the capstone workflow — each applies one of the path's core tools to the project dataset. They read as variants of one idea: using each tool for what it does best in a real analysis. Building the data model is a structural design task that precedes or accompanies tool integration and is better shown separately.

clusters.title: Applying Statistics and Building the Visualization
clusters.reasoning: Applying descriptive statistics and building the dashboard or visualization set are two sequential steps of the capstone's analysis and presentation phase: compute the summaries, then visualize them. The statistics inform what to show; the visualization makes it communicable. They read as two parts of one idea: turning data into insight.

clusters.title: Narrating and Delivering the Capstone
clusters.reasoning: The narrated stakeholder summary and the documented/presented deliverable are two forms of the same final output: communicating the capstone results. The narration is the verbal presentation; the documentation is the written artifact. They read as two aspects of one idea: delivering the completed analysis to a stakeholder. Independent execution is the process of doing the work, which is a distinct concept.
